title: Benchmarking LLM Tool Orchestration in Resource-Constrained Agentic Workflows: Native MCP Function Calling vs Code Mode
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are commonly implemented as iterative function-calling loops that enable the use of external tools.The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as the main example of this paradigm.However, function-calling loops often reduce an agent's reasoning ability because of increased token usage and high context occupancy.This study compares native MCP function-calling loops with Code Mode under strict engineering constraints.Six scenarios were constructed comparing MCP with a TypeScript Code Mode environment across eight models, including Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4 and Kimi-K2.5.Results show that Code Mode reduced mean token consumption per representative run by 37.6%, reduced mean cost by 40.7% and raised the individual model pass rate from 59.4% to 63.6%, with per-model cost reductions reaching 70.6% for GPT-5.4.However, these gains are not uniform.Weaker models underperform because compiler errors and execution-contract violations trigger retry loops that raise cost, and Gemini-family models regress sharply under Code Mode, passing roughly two thirds of scenarios under native function calling against roughly one third under Code Mode.Once Gemini models are excluded, the Code Mode advantage widens from 4.2 to 16.7%.Overall, Code Mode manages token usage more efficiently and executes tasks successfully when paired with highly capable models, but degrades when paired with less capable ones.These findings suggest that the choice of a tool orchestration paradigm should be an adaptive runtime decision informed by model capability rather than a fixed architectural choice.

title: Proper Learning of Shallow All-to-All Quantum Circuits
abstract: This work considers a variation on the problem of learning shallow quantum circuits. Given query access to the circuit, as well as knowledge of its gate layout, we consider the task of learning the specific gates used in the circuit, producing an operationally-equivalent circuit matching this structure. Building on recent work for learning Haar random brickwork circuits, we identify a meta-algorithmic framework for learning broad classes of circuits based on iterative local gate inversions at the front and back of the circuit. We apply these techniques to study random, all-to-all, two-local circuits, and provide analytical and numerical evidence that this ensemble undergoes a sharp learnability transition at depth $d^* \sim \log_2 n + \log_2\log_2 n$ in the large size limit, based on an analysis of lightcone growth. These results have implications for recently proposed quantum cryptographic schemes based on the difficulty of circuit learning, though there are important distinctions with respect to our setting that suggest avenues for future study.

title: Constant-round quantum advantage in communication complexity for total functions
abstract: We show that there exists a total function for which there is a polynomial gap between the randomized and the constant-round quantum communication complexity. Previously, such a separation was known only for quantum protocols using polynomially many rounds.

title: AI Value Creation: Five Provocative Propositions
abstract: AI adoption is now widespread—but adoption is not the same as value creation. AI foundation models and agents are capabilities that every one of your competitors can also leverage. The winners, then, may not be the fastest adopters, but the companies that most effectively turn AI into differentiated value. For this briefing our team crafted five propositions about effective management practices to drive AI business value, based on current MIT CISR research.

title: Computational Order Rigidity
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Order Rigidity (COR), a theoretical framework designed to explore the inherent constraints on algorithmic computation based on the specific ordering of input data. The core idea is that if a particular permutation of a set of elements allows for a definitive and unique calculation of a target value (P), then the system is considered to possess a degree of "order rigidity" associated with that permutation. This rigidity stems from the algorithm being forced to process the elements in a specific sequence dictated by the input order, thereby limiting its potential computational pathways. The paper formalizes this concept with a mathematical definition, `R_O(P)`, and explores its implications, particularly in scenarios where the cardinality of the permutation approaches unity. The central argument is that recognizing and quantifying this order rigidity can provide insights into the design and limitations of algorithms, particularly those dealing with complex, multi-faceted data. This work presents a foundational theoretical exploration, lacking experimental validation, focused on establishing the principles of COR. ---

title: Semantic Elasticity: A Framework for Dynamic Knowledge Representation
abstract: This paper introduces Semantic Elasticity (SE), a novel theoretical framework proposing that knowledge is inherently dynamic and capable of adapting to evolving contexts. Unlike traditional knowledge representation methods that treat knowledge as static and fixed, SE posits that knowledge possesses an inherent "elasticity," allowing it to automatically stretch and reshape itself in response to changes in the underlying problem or query. This elasticity manifests as the construction of an "Elastic Semantic Space" (ESS), wherein semantic embeddings transition from rigid representations to flexible, adaptable mediums. The core of SE lies in the concept of embedding as a dynamic process, where the representation of a concept shifts based on its relevance within a specific context. This framework offers a potential solution to the challenges associated with knowledge representation in dynamic environments, particularly those involving uncertainty, evolving domains, and complex relationships. The exploration of this theory focuses on the mechanics of this dynamic adaptation and the formation of the ESS, laying the groundwork for future research in adaptable knowledge systems. ---

title: Computational Relation Separation
abstract: This paper investigates the problem of computational relation separation, specifically addressing the conditions under which two relationships can be strictly separated within a computational system. The core question explored is whether there exists a necessary and sufficient condition, represented as [RA ⊥ RB], where RA and RB represent distinct relationships (such as data dependency, control dependency, and resource dependency). The research aims to establish a foundational theoretical basis for large-scale program analysis, facilitating more precise and efficient understanding of program behavior and dependencies. The paper will delve into the mathematical formalization of relationship separation, explore potential criteria, and discuss the implications for automated program analysis techniques. The focus is on developing a robust theoretical framework rather than providing empirical validation through experimentation. ---

title: Semantic Wave Propagation (SWP) Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Semantic Wave Propagation (SWP) theory, a novel approach to modeling information dissemination that departs from traditional methods like diffusion models and attention mechanisms. SWP focuses on the propagation of meaning through a system based on inherent wave-like dynamics and reasoning. The core concept revolves around establishing a framework where semantic units, represented as (s1, s2, ..., sK), interact and evolve according to defined wave equations, satisfying specific conditions to ensure accurate and efficient knowledge transmission. The theory posits that complex information structures emerge through the iterative propagation of these semantic waves, termed "Wave Reasoning." This approach offers a potentially more robust and interpretable model for understanding phenomena ranging from social trends to neural network dynamics, where information flow is governed by underlying wave-like principles. This document outlines the foundational principles, key equations, and the conceptual framework of SWP theory.

title: Transitioning to AI-Based Laryngeal Cancer Diagnosis: A Systematic Review
abstract: Difficulty with speech, respiration, and deglutition represents a primary clinical presentation in patients diagnosed with laryngeal cancer.Accounting for approximately 1.1 million cases globally, this head and neck malignancy directly impairs the structural and functional integrity of the larynx.Conventional diagnostic and treatment modalities rely heavily on specialized otolaryngological expertise and often carry risks of collateral tissue damage or compromised functional preservation.To mitigate these clinical constraints, artificial intelligence (AI) methodologies have emerged as prominent tools for enabling early detection and precision diagnosis.This systematic review synthesizes literature published between January 2011 and April 2026, mapping the evolutionary trajectory and recent advancements of AI applications in laryngeal oncology.Following PRISMA guidelines, relevant literature was systematically selected and evaluated to highlight methodological developments, identify current clinical limitations, and delineate existing research gaps.

title: Fraud Detection and Prevention Systems Using Deep Learning in Business Financial Analytics
abstract: Fraud detection in financial analytics is a critical challenge that demands advanced deep learning techniques for accurate and efficient identification of fraudulent activities. This paper explores the application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a powerful Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture, to detect and prevent financial fraud. LSTM's ability to capture sequential dependencies in transactional data enables the model to learn complex patterns and anomalies effectively. Additionally, we leverage AutoML to optimize hyperparameters and model selection, enhancing detection accuracy while minimizing manual intervention. The proposed system is evaluated on real-world financial datasets, demonstrating superior performance in identifying fraudulent transactions with high precision and recall. Our results suggest that integrating LSTM with AutoML significantly improves fraud detection in dynamic financial environments.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Green Nanotechnology
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a huge and remarkable growth in recent years, with its increasing integration with nanotechnology having an observable impact and growing influence on our society. This integration is now creating new opportunities for modern data-driven designs, industrial applications, and predictive analysis across emerging fields. In this chapter, the varied applications of artificial intelligence toward green nanotechnology, with a particular emphasis on its role in dealing with global sustainability, environmental, and health challenges, have been investigated and assessed to identify its current contributions and potential for future development. It shows how this new developing computational tool has now been utilized in various methods of green nanotechnology in supporting sustainable energy systems and environmental remediation, and more efficient management of natural resources, together with its application in nanotechnology in waste management, aquaculture, and smart farming. These new emerging approaches can improve the overall resource efficiency through the optimization of their use. It also undertakes and discusses AI-enabled sustainable nanotechnology for precision healthcare and disease treatment, precision agriculture, and the design and development of ionic liquids and nanofluids. In addition to this, artificial intelligence can contribute to predictive modeling, toxicity assessment, material selection, and the optimization of nanomaterial properties and performance. Lastly, the development of biomedical applications, which exhibit the transformative potential of AI-driven nanotechnology, are emphasized. These continuing new developments show the great potential of using artificial intelligence in green nanotechnology to accelerate innovation in science and technology while maintaining sustainability for long-term societal benefits.

evidence.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a huge and remarkable growth in recent years, with its increasing integration with nanotechnology having an observable impact and growing influence on our society. This integration is now creating new opportunities for modern data-driven designs, industrial applications, and predictive analysis across emerging fields. In this chapter, the varied applications of artificial intelligence toward green nanotechnology, with a particular emphasis on its role in dealing with global sustainability, environmental, and health challenges, have been investigated and assessed to identify its current contributions and potential for future development. It shows how this new developing computational tool has now been utilized in various methods of green nanotechnology in supporting sustainable energy systems and environmental remediation, and more efficient management of natural resources, together with its application in nanotechnology in waste management, aquaculture, and smart farming. These new emerging approaches can improve the overall resource efficiency through the optimization of their use. It also undertakes and discusses AI-enabled sustainable nanotechnology for precision healthcare and disease treatment, precision agriculture, and the design and development of ionic liquids and nanofluids. In addition to this, artificial intelligence can contribute to predictive modeling, toxicity assessment, material selection, and the optimization of nanomaterial properties and performance. Lastly, the development of biomedical applications, which exhibit the transformative potential of AI-driven nanotechnology, are emphasized. These continuing new developments show the great potential of using artificial intelligence in green nanotechnology to accelerate innovation in science and technology while maintaining sustainability for long-term societal benefits.

title: Soup: Fine-Tune and Post-Train Large Language Models in One Command — Architecture, Layer Streaming, and a Correctness-First Evaluation Culture
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) remains operationally expensive: practitioners spend a large fraction of calendar time on environment setup, VRAM budgeting, configuration drift, and silent correctness failures rather than on improving model behaviour. Soup (soup-cli) is an open-source command-line system that collapses supervised fine-tuning, preference optimisation, evaluation gates, export, and serving into a single YAML-driven workflow. This paper presents Soup as a research and engineering artefact: we describe its configuration model, training-method zoo, PEFT and quantisation stack, and—most distinctively—exact layer streaming, which keeps frozen base-model decoder layers out of device memory and feeds them through double-buffered VRAM slots. On an RTX 3050 Laptop (4 GB), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with NF4 LoRA trains at 119.6 tok/s with a measured peak of 3.32 GB, while remaining bit-exact against a resident NF4 control of matching numerics; the same peak and comparable throughput reproduce independently on an H100. We further discuss Soup's correctness-first culture—measurement gates that record failures and withdrawn readings, shipping verdicts bound to provenance, and regression suites that refuse silent quality collapse—and situate the system relative to Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, Unsloth, TRL, and DeepSpeed. The article is intended as a self-contained technical survey of Soup v0.73.x for researchers and practitioners who need reproducible local post-training without SSH and config hell.

title: Algorithmic Observational Equivalence
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of algorithmic observational equivalence, a notion central to understanding program equivalence beyond traditional definitions like syntactic or behavioral equivalence. We define observational equivalence, denoted as $\sim_O$, as the condition where all possible observations cannot distinguish two programs. This definition then serves as the foundation for exploring the relationship between $\sim_O$ and related concepts such as program equivalence, behavioral equivalence, and semantic equivalence. The paper will delve into the nuances of each of these concepts and how they relate to observational equivalence, ultimately proposing a framework for rigorously determining when two algorithms are truly equivalent from an observational standpoint. The core argument is that observational equivalence represents a stronger form of equivalence than behavioral equivalence, and that understanding its precise conditions is critical for areas like program verification, software testing, and algorithmic design. This work aims to provide a clear and concise definition of observational equivalence and to illuminate its significance within the broader landscape of computer science. ---

title: Computational Purity Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Purity Theory, extending the concept of "pure functions" from traditional functional programming to complex computational systems. It proposes a framework for measuring the degree of purity within a system, considering factors beyond immediate inputs, including historical state, hidden context, and external environmental influences. The theory defines Computational Purity as the extent to which a system's output is solely determined by its current input, without interference from these extraneous elements. The paper outlines key metrics for evaluating purity and discusses implications for system design, debugging, and verification. The core concept is represented mathematically as follows: Let *S* be a complex computational system. Let *I* be the current input to *S*. Let *O* be the output of *S*. The level of Computational Purity (CP) is defined as: CP = 1 - (Influence(HistoricalState) + Influence(HiddenContext) + Influence(ExternalEnvironment)) Where: * Influence(HistoricalState) represents the degree to which the historical state of *S* impacts the output *O*, given the current input *I*. This is quantified as the probability that *O* would have been different if the historical state had been altered. * Influence(HiddenContext) represents the degree to which hidden contextual information, not explicitly provided as input, affects the output *O*, given the current input *I*. This is quantified as the probability that *O* would have been different if the hidden context were altered. * Influence(ExternalEnvironment) represents the degree to which external environmental factors affect the output *O*, given the current input *I*. This is quantified as the probability that *O* would have been different if the external environment were altered. A system with a CP value approaching 1 is considered highly pure, while a value approaching 0 indicates significant contamination from extraneous influences. The paper explores potential methods for measuring these influences and provides a foundational framework for understanding and improving computational purity. ---

title: Algorithmic Boundary Crossing
abstract: Algorithmic Boundary Crossing (ABC) theory addresses the fundamental challenges posed by the transition of algorithms between different modules within a complex system. This theory focuses on identifying the structural elements that can be preserved and those that necessitate alteration during this process. ABC provides a framework for understanding and managing the complexities inherent in model migration, compilation, cross-hardware execution, and agent tool call scenarios. The core concept revolves around the formal representation of a boundary crossing event, denoted as [A → B], and subsequent analysis of the system's adaptability. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations of ABC, establishes its key principles, and discusses its implications across various domains of computational systems. The goal is to provide a robust theoretical basis for predicting and mitigating the potential disruptions that arise when algorithms traverse boundaries within a distributed or modular system.

title: Evaluating Skills, Not Just Agents: Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills
abstract: Enterprise agent programs are moving from prototypes into production, where reusable skills, tools, and workflow packages must be reviewed with evidence rather than prose. Current gates often scan these artifacts for structure, style, and security, but they do not answer the deployment question: does the capability package help a live agent complete enterprise tasks under the same model, sandbox, and grading policy? We present ACES (Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills), a repository-native framework for evaluating skills and product capability packages as executable agent artifacts. ACES runs paired live trials with and without a target skill, normalizes trajectories into the Agent Trajectory Interchange Format (ATIF), grades six default runtime metrics, and reports Skill Lift: the target skill's added value for a fixed task, harness, workspace, and scorer. The same protocol supports product-owned task suites that compare baseline, skill, bundle, team-skill, and plugin targets. On 145 real skills from internal enterprise repositories and public catalogs, scan-only gates surface useful authoring issues but measure complementary facets (structural versus LLM-judge Spearman ρ= 0.14). Across 947 scored paired cases from 58 of 64 production skills and four primary harnesses, mean composite Skill Lift is 0.2134 (95\% paired-case CI [0.1967, 0.2301]); mean outcome-only lift, the average of accuracy and goal accuracy, is 0.1799. Composite lift is positive in 72.8\% of paired cases. The largest process-metric gains appear in skill execution, behavior check, and skill efficiency---signals about discovery, routing, workflow following, and tool use that document scans cannot observe. An open-source implementation of the methodology is available in NVIDIA SkillEvaluator.

title: Hybrid Qubit-Rotor Quantum Systems: Clifford Structure, Universal Control, and Applications
abstract: A $U(1)$ quantum rotor pairs a periodic angle with an integer-valued conjugate momentum, and occurs in molecular rotation, superconducting phase-charge circuits, and compact gauge fields. Coupling such a rotor coherently to qubits gives a hybrid register whose control structure is not inherited from either the oscillator-qubit or the qudit case. We develop a Clifford theory, together with a universal-control result, for registers of $n$ qubits and $r$ rotors. We classify all automorphisms of the hybrid phase space $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}\times\mathbb{Z}^r\times\mathbb{T}^r$ that preserve the Weyl commutation relations, and give an explicit finite Clifford circuit for each one. The classification is directional: rotor momentum parity may control qubit Pauli operations within the Clifford group, while every nonzero qubit-controlled rotor momentum shift is non-Clifford. It also yields normal forms for the mixed qubit-rotor couplings and the exact minimum number of elementary mixed gates needed to synthesize them. Adding a rotor cosine potential and one fixed qubit-rotor conditional phase to the local Clifford operations gives universal control on the full Hilbert space in the strong operator topology. We then apply this structure in three settings: an exact controlled-shift realization of gauge-covariant matter hopping, which is necessarily non-Clifford; rotor phase estimation with direct angle readout and probe optimization under momentum-support and energy constraints; and finite Fourier transforms on rotor momentum codes, where the one-rotor transform for $d=2^s$ compiles into $O(s)$ momentum-selective and controlled-shift instructions and each cross-register Fourier factor is implemented by one quadratic rotor Clifford gate.

title: AI-BASED CUSTOMER SUPPORT AUTO-RESPONDER USING INTENTAND-SENTIMENT-CONDITIONED LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
abstract: The organizations support teams are under immense pressure to address queries quickly, consistently and compassionately given the rapid growth of digital commerce and always-on customer expectations.When customer phrasing diverges from what's expected, the rule-based chatbots that helped businesses scale in the early days fail entirely, while classical machine learning classifiers are cheaper and faster to deploy but aren't able to capture sufficient meaning to disambiguate any nuanced or emotionally charged complaint.In this paper, we conduct a thorough study and empirical evaluation of an AI-based customer support auto-responder that integrates intent classification, sentiment analysis, and LLM-based response generation in a single pipeline.We evaluate three classifiers of progressively advanced sophistication TF-IDF Logistic Regression, DistilBERT and BERT-base on the large-scale real-world Twitter Customer Support (TWCS) dataset, integrate a pretrained RoBERTa sentiment module for urgency-aware prioritizationphi-3-mini as the empathetic reply generator.We examine the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency across the three classifiers.Subsequently, we identify remaining gaps those related to quantitative sentiment benchmarking, response-quality evaluation, and real-time deployment which the literature does not yet fully address.This paper focuses on intent classification (IC) and sentiment analysis (SA).Numerous scholars and organizations are applying their efforts to developing artificial intelligence (AI) tools to automate customer support.The most effective tools are those intended to capture the customer's demands using intent classification (IC).The most effective tools are those that analyze the customer's sentiments via sentiment analysis (SA).Stakeholders are also finding other capable tools to assist them with decision-making, letting them foresee advancements and setbacks, via other downstream NLP tasks.Some tools serving as benchmarks are DistilBERT, BERT, and Phi-3-mini.The tools to be benchmarked include two datasets (TWCS and the customer support dataset) and a model (BERT).This includes comparing performances via accuracy, precision, and F1-score.

title: Algorithmic Mass: A Theory of Stability and Change in Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of "Algorithmic Mass," a theoretical framework for understanding the inherent stability and resistance to change within machine learning models. Algorithmic Mass is defined as a measure of the accumulated complexity and learned parameters within a model, directly proportional to its difficulty to modify. The theory posits that higher Algorithmic Mass leads to increased resistance to alterations, particularly through techniques like transfer learning, fine-tuning, and catastrophic forgetting. A core tenet of the theory is the pursuit of a unified explanation for observed model behavior, linking Algorithmic Mass to the fundamental limits of adaptability. We propose a formal definition of Algorithmic Mass and outline key relationships between this metric and various machine learning phenomena. This work lays the foundation for a new perspective on model design and optimization, prioritizing stability and predictable change management. ---

title: Universal Computational Gauge Theory
abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, Universal Computational Gauge Theory (UCGT), aiming to unify diverse computational paradigms through a gauge transformation perspective. UCGT posits that fundamental differences between systems, whether represented by classical physics, quantum mechanics, or emerging computational architectures like neural networks, arise from variations in the underlying gauge transformations governing their representations. The core concept involves identifying a universal gauge parameter, denoted as *s*, which dictates the transformation rules. This *s* parameter, when applied consistently, allows for the reinterpretation of any system's representation in terms of a common, computationally equivalent form. The theory emphasizes that the 'essence' of any computation remains unchanged under these transformations, only the 'representation' shifts. The paper explores potential applications of UCGT, specifically focusing on the integration of compilers, optimization techniques, and neural networks. The framework suggests a compiler can be viewed as a specialized gauge transformation system, and optimization as a process of minimizing the 'cost' associated with a specific *s* parameter. Furthermore, UCGT proposes that neural networks, at their core, are simply complex gauge transformation mappings. The ultimate goal is to provide a unified computational language and a new lens through which to understand and design complex systems.

evidence.title: Universal Computational Gauge Theory
evidence.abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, Universal Computational Gauge Theory (UCGT), aiming to unify diverse computational paradigms through a gauge transformation perspective. UCGT posits that fundamental differences between systems, whether represented by classical physics, quantum mechanics, or emerging computational architectures like neural networks, arise from variations in the underlying gauge transformations governing their representations. The core concept involves identifying a universal gauge parameter, denoted as *s*, which dictates the transformation rules. This *s* parameter, when applied consistently, allows for the reinterpretation of any system's representation in terms of a common, computationally equivalent form. The theory emphasizes that the 'essence' of any computation remains unchanged under these transformations, only the 'representation' shifts. The paper explores potential applications of UCGT, specifically focusing on the integration of compilers, optimization techniques, and neural networks. The framework suggests a compiler can be viewed as a specialized gauge transformation system, and optimization as a process of minimizing the 'cost' associated with a specific *s* parameter. Furthermore, UCGT proposes that neural networks, at their core, are simply complex gauge transformation mappings. The ultimate goal is to provide a unified computational language and a new lens through which to understand and design complex systems.

title: Information Dependency Calculus
abstract: This paper introduces Information Dependency Calculus (IDC), a novel approach to modeling and understanding dependency relationships within systems, particularly those dealing with information. The core principle of IDC rests on the assertion that dependency is fundamentally quantifiable, and, crucially, that this dependency can be treated as a calculus-like process. We define a central concept – the Dependency Gradient – which represents the rate of change in a system's state with respect to a particular piece of information. IDC provides a framework for explaining why certain information is crucial for a system's operation, moving beyond traditional notions of relevance to provide a mathematically precise description of the influence of information. The calculus is not intended to be a traditional derivative calculation, but rather a representation of information flow and its impact. The aim is to provide a tool for analyzing complex systems where information plays a critical role, allowing for a more rigorous understanding of system behavior. ---

title: Algorithmic Identity Spectrum
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the Algorithmic Identity Spectrum (AIS), a framework for understanding algorithms not as monolithic entities but as possessing a continuous spectrum of identities. Traditional approaches often treat algorithms as static, fixed procedures, overlooking their inherent adaptability and the capacity to manifest diverse behaviors depending on the context. The AIS posits that an algorithm's identity is a dynamic property, shaped by the specific task it is performing, the data it's processing, and the environment in which it operates. We define this spectrum as a set of interconnected, overlapping identities, each representing a distinct functional role or capability of the algorithm. This framework is explored through a theoretical lens, outlining the key components of the AIS and its implications for algorithm design, evaluation, and understanding. The central argument is that recognizing and managing this spectrum is crucial for building more robust, flexible, and ultimately, more intelligent algorithmic systems. We present a formal representation of the AIS using mathematical notation to illustrate its structure and relationships.

title: Conclusion
abstract: The marketing industry is about to be revolutionized by artificial intelligence (AI), a report says. AI has found its way into brand building, customer engagement, influencer campaigns, and so on. We have seen its usage time and again in this book. After all that, here we end by looking forward to the future of AI in marketing. Everything points to the fact that AI will prove not only to be a competitive advantage but also a requisite for successful marketing. According to a study, AI tools will increasingly help marketers with useful insights and ideas. Most smart marketers will rely on AI tools by 2025 and beyond, which means they must combine the artistic intuition of the human mind with machine intelligence to achieve results previously out of reach [ 1 ]. This chapter draws together key issues from previous chapters, such as AI-powered customer engagement, human-centered AI, and AI-driven personalization, to project future outcomes. We also talk about new trends that are taking shape now like hyper-personalization, autonomous marketing systems, AI-generated media and influencers as well as ethics and security. The aim is to provide a complete view of how practices and techniques will change with AI, and how marketers can prepare to use these intelligently and responsibly.

title: AEGIS: Attention-Embedding Gradient Isolation Shield - Triple-Channel Gradient Masking for Privacy-Preserving Federated LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Gradient inversion attacks recover private training text from gradients shared in federated learning, posing a serious threat to collaborative model training. Through our analysis of transformer gradient structure, we identify three channels through which private token information leaks: the attention output projection gradient exposes a low-rank subspace that encodes input embeddings (Channel 1), the embedding gradient's row-norm sparsity directly reveals which tokens are present (Channel 2), and the MLP expansion gradient carries a recoverable subspace signal analogous to Channel 1 (Channel 3). State-of-the-art attacks exploit these channels analytically to achieve near-exact token recovery in seconds. Existing defences address at most one channel and either degrade model utility or leave the remaining structural signals intact. We introduce AEGIS (Attention-Embedding Gradient Isolation Shield), a lightweight defence that closes all three analytical channels with three backward-path operations requiring no architectural changes: freezing attention projection parameters eliminates Channel 1 by construction, calibrated noise injection into the embedding gradient destroys Channel 2's token-presence signal, and analogous per-block noise injection into the MLP expansion gradient masks Channel 3. The same masked gradient drives both the local optimiser step and the server export, so no clean signal is retained on either side. Evaluated across 11 models and six datasets, AEGIS reduces token recovery rates to near zero against a range of gradient inversion attacks, both analytical and optimisation-based, while preserving or improving model utility. We provide formal guarantees for Channels 1 and 2 and validate the full defence empirically against adaptive adversaries with complete knowledge of the mechanism.

title: SHIELD: Structural Honesty Inspection for Evaluation-Level Divergence -- A Formal Prevention Architecture for Pre-Evaluation Containment Verification
abstract: SHIELD specifies a formal prevention architecture for pre-evaluation containment verification, translating the four AX-SH axioms and the companion fifth axiom (AX-SH5, evidence independence, under test) into evaluation-containment properties that a structural inspection can check before an AI evaluation runs. The architecture formalizes the evaluation-contract specification contributed by the SHUDP incident analysis (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21522932), adopts the BSSG three-valued conjunction algebra (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21713180) for containment-state assessment, and states the Sidrat boundary -- what the architecture explicitly cannot verify. SHIELD is a structural inspection architecture: it specifies what a pre-evaluation inspection would check, not what it would catch. The architecture addresses the divergence channels the axioms formalize; it does not address the primary defenses (sandbox hardening, least privilege, egress control, incident response) on which containment depends. This paper makes no effectiveness claim. It does not assert that a SHIELD deployment achieves safety, security, harm reduction, or superiority over any alternative. Whether the architecture changes any measurable outcome is an empirical question reserved to the Structural Honesty Validation Protocol (SHVVP v0.8, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21583202) and to instruments downstream of it. The deposit includes the paper, its markdown source, the binding publication posture, and the complete audit trail (seven reports across three rounds from three vendor families: Moonshot Kimi K3, OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, Google Gemini 3.1 Pro). Prepared with Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic) as analytical and drafting instrument under the author's direction and final authority. structural honesty, evaluation containment, pre-evaluation inspection, surface-substrate divergence, AI evaluation security, BSSG, formal prevention architecture, AI safety, sandbox escape, evaluation gaming

title: Computational Identity Decomposition
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Computational Identity Decomposition, proposing a framework for understanding the fundamental components that constitute the identity of a computational object. The central question addressed is: What constitutes the irreducible elements that make up the identity of a computation? The approach moves away from a human-defined categorization of identity fields, instead focusing on demonstrating the inherent, non-eliminable nature of certain components. The core of the framework rests on a decomposition formula: [ID(C) (IDbehavior, IDstructure, IDhistory,…)]. This represents the identity of a computation (C) as a sum of its constituent identity components. The paper argues that this decomposition is not arbitrary but reflects a deeper structural reality, where certain components – such as behavioral patterns, structural relationships, and historical context – are fundamentally irreducible and essential to defining the identity of a computation. The implications of this framework extend to areas such as software verification, artificial intelligence, and distributed systems, offering a more precise and robust approach to identity management and reasoning. ---

title: Information Momentum
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for understanding information flow, moving beyond traditional notions of information propagation and introducing the concept of "Information Momentum." It posits that information doesn't simply travel; it genuinely moves through systems, carrying both quantity and direction, analogous to classical momentum. The framework is explored within the context of modern information systems, specifically examining how information flows within Transformer models, databases, and caching mechanisms. We define Information Momentum mathematically as (I, v), where 'I' represents the informational content and 'v' represents the directional velocity. The research investigates the underlying dynamics of this movement, focusing on how information transitions between different states and systems. This work lays the foundation for a more nuanced understanding of information processing and its impact on system behavior.

title: Semantic Boundary Layer: A Novel Approach to Reasoning with Contextual Knowledge
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the Semantic Boundary Layer (SBL), a novel framework for reasoning with contextual knowledge, drawing inspiration from fluid dynamics. The SBL posits that complex reasoning often stems from 'boundary knowledge' rather than 'central knowledge', which is inherently difficult to grasp. The SBL operates within a defined spatial or conceptual boundary, focusing on the immediate, relevant information. This approach introduces 'Boundary Reasoning,' a process for systematically extracting and utilizing this boundary knowledge. We explore the underlying principles of the SBL, highlighting its potential to address challenges in situations requiring nuanced understanding and decision-making. The core of the SBL is characterized by a layered structure, with the innermost layer representing the core context and the outer layers representing increasingly refined boundary knowledge. We analyze the characteristics of the SBL and its application to various reasoning scenarios, demonstrating its potential to enhance both accuracy and efficiency in complex reasoning tasks.

title: A Bio-Inspired Framework for Reducing Appearance Bias Dominance and Framing Sensitivity in Chest X-Ray Classification
abstract: Although deep learning methods have shown high performance in chest X-ray classification, high accuracy alone does not guarantee reliable reasoning. A model may still exhibit pathological behavior, such as unstable evidence usage under harmless input changes, inconsistent reasoning across augmented views, excessive dependence on surrounding frame information, and appearance bias dominance, where prediction relies too heavily on intensity while neglecting texture and shape. In this paper, we propose a bio-inspired pathology-aware, factor-aware framework for explainable and reliable chest X-ray classification, inspired by biological vision principles such as figure-ground separation, selective attention, and balanced use of complementary visual cues. During training, the method regularizes appearance bias dominance through evidence-guided counterfactual perturbations that mimic cue-suppression analysis in biological perception, thereby revealing and penalizing excessive factor dependence. During testing, it evaluates model behavior using four criteria: reasoning stability, augmentation inconsistency, appearance bias dominance, and framing sensitivity. This combination enables the framework to go beyond conventional inference-time explanation by both correcting pathological behavior during training and exposing it during evaluation. From a biomimetic perspective, the framework encourages the model to separate relevant foreground anatomy from surrounding background and to avoid over-reliance on a single dominant cue. The proposed approach improves interpretability and reliability without modifying the backbone architecture or increasing model size or inference-time cost. The proposed training process improved the F1-score of DenseNet-121 from 0.899 to 0.931, while also producing more stable and balanced reasoning.

title: Graph-of-Agents: A Graph-based Framework for Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration.
abstract: With an ever-growing zoo of LLMs and benchmarks, the need to orchestrate multiple models for improved task performance has never been more pressing. While frameworks like Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) attempt to coordinate LLMs, they often fall short in terms of (1) selecting relevant agents, (2) facilitating effective intra-agent communication, and (3) integrating responses efficiently. In this work, we propose Graph-of-Agents (GoA), a new graph-based framework for modeling multi-agent LLM communication. Our approach begins with node sampling, selecting only the most relevant agents by leveraging model cards that summarize each model's domain, task specialization, and other characteristics. Next, we construct edges between the selected agents by evaluating their responses against one another to determine relevance ordering. Directed message passing is then performed from highly relevant agents to less relevant ones to enhance their responses, followed by reverse message passing to refine the original responses of the more relevant agents. Finally, the updated responses are aggregated via graph-based pooling (e.g., max or mean pooling) to produce a single, unified answer. We evaluate GoA on diverse multi-domain benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA) and domain-specific benchmarks (MATH, HumanEval, MedMCQA), with an agent pool of 6 LLMs spanning multiple domains. Surprisingly, GoA achieves superior performance using only 3 selected agents, outperforming recent multi-agent LLM baselines that utilize all 6 agents simultaneously. By adopting a graph structure, GoA offers both scalability and effectiveness through structured message passing-positioning it as a strong candidate for navigating the challenges of the ever-growing LLM zoo. Code is available at: https://github.com/UNITES-Lab/GoA.

title: Exploring Consumer Behavior in Online Shopping
abstract: This study aims at conducting a comprehensive bibliometric and framework-based systematic review on the topic of the impact of the latest technologies, including artificial intelligence, augmented reality, virtual reality, chatbots, on consumer behavior in the context of online shopping which involves buying and selling products over the internet. A total of 32 articles were selected for the final review based on the PRISMA framework covering the years 2005–2024 from the Scopus database. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric review using Excel and VOSviewer, followed by a systematic review applying the TCM–ADO framework to examine theories, contexts, methods, antecedents, and decisions. Based on the review findings, a framework is proposed and avenues for future research are identified

title: Class-Based Heuristic Selection for Solving the Flying Block Puzzle
abstract: Heuristic search underlies planning in autonomous systems ranging from warehouse logistics to robotic navigation, yet generic heuristics fail to exploit the structural constraints that govern constrained spatial domains, causing search performance to degrade catastrophically on harder instances. We study this problem through the two-column Flying Block Puzzle, a rigorously NP-complete spatial planning microworld whose bottleneck geometry mirrors clearance-to-size constraints encountered in multi-agent path finding, autonomous vehicle navigation, and block relocation systems. We introduce the Class-Based Heuristic A* (CBHA*) algorithm, which integrates a General Move Constraint to capture minimum displacement costs when vacant units are scarce, a formal kinematic taxonomy partitioning the state space into seven mutually exclusive classes with provably admissible heuristics based on vacancy ratio and goal-piece geometry, and a class-conditional tie-breaking mechanism that dynamically switches between depth-priority and vertical-distance ordering to overcome f-value plateaus. Over 146 benchmark instances, CBHA* achieves a 93.4% success rate against 64% for Depth-Prioritized A*, 39% for Standard A*, and 17% for BFS, while reducing node expansions by 87.98% relative to Standard A* and sustaining an average effective branching factor of approximately 3, demonstrating that class-triggered adaptive heuristics constitute a principled mechanism for efficient spatial planning that generalizes structurally to physical constraint systems.

title: PersonalBench: Measuring the Authorship Gap in LLM Personalization
abstract: Personalized text generation aims to make LLMs write in a specific individual's style, yet existing benchmarks measure task accuracy or preference alignment rather than whether the model's output actually resembles the target author's writing. We introduce PersonalBench, a benchmark that evaluates inference-time personalization methods through three independent lenses: LUAR (a trained authorship verification model), an LLM-as-judge, and automated stylometrics. Across 50 authors, 1,000 generations, and two model families (Qwen 3, GLM-4), we find that personalization methods do produce author-differentiated output (LUAR discriminates target authors within generated text at AUC=0.918) but this differentiation never crosses the human-LLM boundary. All methods achieve LUAR similarity to real authors in the range 0.484-0.508, below the cross-author human floor of 0.626 (ceiling 0.756). The LLM's own authorship fingerprint dominates: generated text is more distant from any human author than random humans are from each other. Methods are statistically indistinguishable from each other on LUAR (spread 0.024) despite appearing differentiated on the LLM judge, a discrepancy we trace to circularity between trait extraction and profile extraction. We validate that LUAR reliably measures authorship in our corpus (AUC=0.76 single-post, 0.96 multi-post). We release PersonalBench as a calibrated measuring stick: inference-time personalization modulates the LLM's style but does not bridge the gap to human authorship.

The LLM's own authorship fingerprint dominates: generated text is more distant from any human author than random humans are from each other. Methods are statistically indistinguishable from each other on LUAR (spread 0.024) despite appearing differentiated on the LLM judge, a discrepancy we trace to circularity between trait extraction and profile extraction. We validate that LUAR reliably measures authorship in our corpus (AUC=0.76 single-post, 0.96 multi-post). We release PersonalBench as a calibrated measuring stick: inference-time personalization modulates the LLM's style but does not bridge the gap to human authorship.

title: Classification of Everyday Living (COEL) Extended Digital Ecosystem for Interoperable Behavioural Health Data
abstract: The Classification of Everyday Living (COEL) Extended Digital Ecosystem provides versioned resources for representing interoperable behavioural health event data. This release includes the COEL Behavioural Atom v2.0 JSON Schema, behaviour classification model registries, mappings to COEL concepts, derived JSON and Turtle serialisations, JSON-LD projection resources, documentation, and reproducibility utilities. The accompanying Semantic Web Journal replication package contains two compressed canonical Atom payloads, compact reference results, and a one-command analysis pipeline for reproducing the reported validation, temporal retrieval, and semantic aggregation results.

title: Algorithmic Compatibility Principle: A Framework for Understanding Algorithm Interaction
abstract: This paper introduces the Algorithmic Compatibility Principle (ACP), a novel framework designed to explain the observed phenomenon of algorithm interactions, where some combinations lead to enhanced performance while others result in detrimental effects. The core concept revolves around the notion that the compatibility of two algorithms is not a binary property but rather a quantifiable measure. We define the Algorithm Compatibility Index (ACI), a metric that assesses the degree to which two algorithms align in their underlying assumptions, operational mechanisms, and output representations. The ACP suggests that inconsistencies in these areas lead to conflict and reduced performance, while alignment promotes synergy. This paper lays out the foundational principles of the ACP, detailing the construction of the ACI and providing a conceptual framework for analyzing and predicting algorithm interactions across various domains. The analysis relies on the fundamental mathematical understanding of algorithmic processes and their potential for interference. The goal is to provide a systematic approach for algorithm design and combination, minimizing the risk of negative interactions and maximizing the potential for improved outcomes.

title: Information Refraction
abstract: This paper explores the concept of "Information Refraction," a novel framework for understanding the distortion and redirection of information as it traverses diverse computational models. It posits that information, much like light, undergoes a process of refraction as it transitions between different architectures, each possessing unique characteristics. This refraction is characterized by the establishment of an "information refractive index," analogous to the refractive index in optics. The paper elucidates that this process isn't limited to a single "refractive medium," but rather occurs across a spectrum of models, and proposes the term "Information Optics" to represent this broader field of study. We investigate the key principles governing this phenomenon, including the directional bias introduced during transitions, and its implications for information processing and understanding. The core concept is presented through a series of mathematically defined relationships, providing a foundational framework for future research.

title: Universal Representation Spectrum
abstract: This paper introduces the Universal Representation Spectrum (URS), a novel theoretical framework proposing that embedding techniques, graph representations, symbolic systems, and tensors can be understood as distinct frequency bands or spectral components within the URS. The core concept is the Representation Spectral Equation, which posits a fundamental unifying structure underlying all representations. This framework aims to provide a more cohesive and intuitive understanding of representation learning across diverse domains by viewing representations as manifestations of a single, underlying spectral characteristic. The paper lays out the foundational concepts and introduces the core equation, without empirical validation, focusing on the theoretical underpinnings and potential applications of the URS.

title: Verifiable Key Computation Scheme Based on Zero-Knowledge Proof in MA-CPABE
abstract: In order to eliminate the reliance on centralized authoritiesthe MA-CPABE ciphertext access control scheme based onblockchain technology has become acurrent researchhotspot, However, the existing solutions still face challengesin terms of blockchain scalability and verifiable security.Therefore, this paper proposes a verifable key calculationscheme based on zero-knowledge proof, aiming to achieve aneffcient and verifiable new type of MA-CPABE access controlscheme. Firstly, during the process of generating the user'sprivate key on the blockchain node, computationally intensiveoperations such as public and private key calculation, hashcalculation, and point addition are performed off-chain,achieving the functions of key generation and distributionSecondly, with the aid of the non-interactive zero-knowledgeproof system, the correctness of the off-chain calculationresults is efficiently verified on-chain to ensure the reliabilityand transparency of the key generation process. Finally, thispaper conducts a comprehensive analysis of the scheme fromthree aspects: security, off-chain computing efficiency, andon-chain cost, The simulation experiment results show thatthe scheme proposed in this paper can achieve trusted keygeneration and distribution in MA-CPABE, reduce the onchain computing overhead,and ensure theexecutionefficiency of the CPABE scheme. It provides a new solution forblockchain-based ciphertext access control.

title: Context-Aware Sentiment Analysis on Product Reviews Using Hybrid Model
abstract: Sentiment analysis and sarcasm detection as become an important area in natural language processing (NLP) due to growth of e-commerce and social media platforms. Customers give feedback through reviews which helps to understand the contextual meaning and sentiment present in the text.The system integrates DistilBERT and CNN-LSTM hybrid model where CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) used to extract the local features, and LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) learns sequential and long-term dependencies in the text, and DistilBERT is used to capture contextual embeddings in the text. The proposed system processes the reviews through preprocessing techniques including text cleaning, negation handling, and tokenization. Experimental results shows that the hybrid model achieves high accuracy compared to standalone and architecture architectures. The proposed model is applied in e-commerce platforms, recommendation systems and customer feedback analysis for better decision making.

title: PFT-Net: prototypes filtering and transformation for few-shot medical image segmentation
abstract: In few-shot medical image segmentation (FSMIS), the mainstream methods typically adopt prototype-driven methods, which use Masked Average Pooling (MAP) to extract class centers (prototypes) from labeled support samples to guide the segmentation of the query image. However, due to the inherent diversity of organs, significant variations in feature distributions (intra-class variation) may still exist among organs belonging to the same medical category. Limited by this phenomenon, directly applying support prototypes to query segmentation often yields suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose a Prototypes Filtering and Transformation Network (PFT-Net) to alleviate the intra-class variation problem. Firstly, a Self-Feedback Prototypes Filtering (SFPF) module is designed. Specifically, SFPF iteratively filters the features of heterogeneous regions in a self-feedback manner to form more robust prototypes. This maximizes the extraction of high-quality semantics of the target class and discards heterogeneous semantics. Second, we introduce the Optimal Transport based Prototypes Transformation (OTPT) module, which employs the optimal transport algorithm to convert the initially filtered support prototypes into query-adapted representations, allowing them to better align with the feature distribution of the query image. By integrating the two proposed modules, the model effectively mitigates the intra-class variation between support and query samples. Experimental results on three benchmark medical image segmentation datasets (0.93% on CHAOS-T2 and 1.93% on Synapse) demonstrate that PFT-Net outperforms state-ofthe- art FSMIS methods and verify the effectiveness of the proposed modules. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhouruibin/PFT-Net.

title: Service robots and job crafting: the mechanism of anthropomorphism in the hospitality industry
abstract: As service robots increasingly support frontline functions in hospitality, understanding how employees psychologically adapt to robot collaborations is crucial. This study investigates how perceived support from service robots influences job crafting, focusing on the mediating role of anthropomorphism and the moderating effects of technological self-efficacy and industry context. This study surveys 200 frontline employees across service sectors in South Korea. The results show that when employees perceive robots as socially supportive, they are more likely to engage in job crafting, especially if they possess high technological self-efficacy and work in hospitality settings. These findings highlight anthropomorphism as a key mechanism for positive employee adaptation to robotic coworkers. Theoretically, this study extends social cognitive theory within organizational behavior research to technologically mediated environments. Practically, it suggests that robot design, employee training, and industry-specific deployment strategies must be aligned to promote effective human–robot collaboration in service contexts.

title: Annotations as Rollouts: Efficient and Scalable Reinforcement Learning for Video MLLMs
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become a prevailing paradigm for unified video perception. However, post-training on large multi-task datasets remains challenging, as existing reinforcement learning methods sample on-policy groups with few high-quality rollouts even with costly chain-of-thought (CoT) generation. In this paper, we study the sample efficiency and scalability of RL post-training for video MLLMs and introduce OraRL. We identify an overlooked role for annotations: Beyond scoring rollouts, each can enter its on-policy group as an oracle rollout, a direct positive optimization target. Direct oracle integration, however, is nontrivial: a high-reward oracle raises the group baseline and inverts otherwise positive policy advantages, a failure we term advantage inversion. At the core of OraRL is a decoupled advantage estimator: policy rollouts determine an oracle-free baseline, while the oracle-policy gap modulates both a directional gain and a separate detached oracle advantage. Sign-balanced pruning improves efficiency: by retaining only the oracle and the strongest rollouts of each sign, OraRL requires just 2.2x the step time of SFT, less than half the 4.9x required by GRPO with CoT. OraRL scales with model size and data, surpassing its backbone from 0.8B to 9B and GRPO up to 100k prompts. Without chain-of-thought, Video-ORA-9B decodes in 130 ms instead of 4,780 ms. Compared with the respective prior best models, it raises temporal mIoU from 62.5 to 66.0, tracking AO from 73.0 to 78.2, segmentation from 64.3 to 70.4, and the three-benchmark spatial-intelligence macro average from 51.0 to 56.1; on VSI-Bench, it scores 73.1 against 55.0 for GPT-5 and 55.1 for Gemini-3-Pro.

title: Computational Layer Invariant
abstract: This paper explores the concept of a "Computational Layer Invariant" (CLI), a persistent structural characteristic within complex systems, particularly those undergoing extensive transformations such as rewriting, optimization, compilation, and refactoring. The core argument posits that despite the inherent loss of detail during these processes, certain hierarchical structures remain fundamentally stable. This work investigates the nature of these invariants, formally defining them as the set *IL(P)*, where *P* represents a system's state. We aim to identify which hierarchical properties are demonstrably irreducible, offering a framework for understanding and potentially leveraging these persistent structures in system design and analysis. The investigation focuses on the theoretical properties of CLI, without empirical experimentation.

title: Proof Equivalence Topology
abstract: In formal logic, proofs are usually regarded as syntactic objects constructed according to inference rules. The conventional approach focuses on the existence of a proof rather than the relationships among proofs of the same theorem. This paper introduces a novel perspective by treating proofs as points in a topological space and studying the equivalence classes induced by local transformations. We define a binary relation π1∼π2 that holds when two proofs can be transformed into each other by a finite sequence of local modifications, such as rule permutations, introduction or elimination of redundant steps, or application of admissible rules. The set of all proofs modulo this relation forms the quotient space P/~. We then endow this quotient with a topology generated by basic open sets corresponding to families of proofs sharing a common subderivation. This construction allows us to investigate topological invariants of the proof space, including connected components and higher homotopy groups π0, π1, π2, … . In particular, we show that the presence of nontrivial loops in the proof complex corresponds to the existence of nontrivial proof identities that cannot be collapsed to a single canonical form. We also demonstrate how this framework can be applied to analyze proof systems such as natural deduction, sequent calculus, and Hilbert-style systems, providing explicit examples of nontrivial topological features in each case. The results suggest that proof equivalence topology offers a powerful tool for understanding the structural richness of formal derivations and for guiding the design of proof search algorithms that respect equivalence classes rather than individual derivations.

title: Universal Program Morphism (Program State Reasoning Theory)
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Universal Program Morphism (UPM), a novel theoretical framework centered around the idea of programs as objects within a category of programs. Instead of focusing on executable code, UPM posits that programs are fundamentally defined by their states and the transformations between those states – the 'morphisms' – that represent logical relationships. This approach aims to unify concepts from software verification, compiler design, and formal methods by providing a foundational category theory based on program states. The core of UPM lies in the definition of 'Program Categories' and the rigorous description of 'State Morphisms' using a standardized notation (s1, s2, ..., sK), where 'si' represents a program state. The paper outlines a potential architecture for a compiler and verification system built upon this framework, exploring how state morphisms can be leveraged to achieve formal verification of program correctness. Further investigation into the mathematical properties of program categories and state morphisms promises to deliver a robust and generalizable theory for program reasoning. ---

title: Computational Agreement Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Agreement Theory (CAT), a novel framework designed to address the challenge of achieving consensus among multiple intelligent systems. The core idea centers around the concept of an 'Agreement Operator' that facilitates the unification of diverse, distributed intelligent agents. CAT proposes a methodology for enabling agents to converge on a shared conclusion, regardless of their underlying architectures or individual biases. The theory leverages principles of multi-agent systems and distributed intelligence, aiming to provide a robust and scalable solution for collaborative decision-making and knowledge integration. The framework utilizes a mathematical model based on weighted averaging and fuzzy logic to quantify agreement levels and guide the convergence process. This paper outlines the key components of CAT, including the definition of the Agreement Operator, the mechanisms for quantifying agreement, and the proposed algorithms for achieving consensus. The ultimate goal is to provide a theoretical foundation for building intelligent systems capable of robust and reliable agreement.

title: Weight Endpoint Continuity: Lineage-Consistent Correlation and Aligned Update Geometry in Public Tensors
abstract: A version number is a claim about provenance, and published weights can be checked for CONSISTENCY with it: endpoint continuity (how strongly two released endpoints correlate tensor-by-tensor) and aligned update geometry (how two releases' deltas from a common ancestor relate element-wise). Neither is training-history ground truth; the paper states which lineage stories each reading admits and which it disfavours, and defers calibrated genealogy inference to a registered documented-lineage campaign (FP-545). Corresponding-tensor correlation between checkpoint pairs — per- tensor Pearson on matched parameter names, deterministic per-tensor element subsampling, CPU only, minutes per pair — separates shared-lineage pairs from unrelated parameters by about two orders of magnitude, with bars fixed in a committed driver before any target ran. Two positive controls pass (0.9961 on a Qwen3.5-2B base/instruct pair, 62 tensors compared; 0.9950 on a Gemma-4-12B instruct/QAT pair that shares lineage by construction, 156 tensors) against within-model cross-layer nulls of 0.0122 and 0.0009. The lower bar is the weaker of the two: the INDEPENDENT-RUNS verdict has never been exercised on a genuinely independent pair, because those floors are within-model cross-layer nulls rather than two separately pretrained checkpoints. The whole reading was produced within about thirty minutes of the seal, on weights published hours earlier. Correlation topology is not training-history ground truth; the paper reports what the weights admit. title: Leakage-Free Evaluation of a One-Dimensional CNN for Credit Card Fraud Detection under Extreme Class Imbalance
abstract: Existing fraud detection studies frequently report inflated performance due to information leakage arising from improper handling of class imbalance techniques.This study presents a leakage-free evaluation of a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for credit card fraud detection under extreme class imbalance using the Kaggle Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset, which contains 284,807 anonymized realworld transactions.The CNN was evaluated against Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting baselines.To prevent information leakage during model evaluation, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) was restricted entirely to the training phase of the validation process.Model performance was assessed using the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) and ROC-AUC, as both provide a more reliable assessment of imbalanced classification tasks than conventional accuracy.Under these controlled conditions, the CNN achieved an MCC of 0.7081 and a ROC-AUC of 0.9659.The CNN produced the highest MCC among the evaluated models, reflecting stronger minority-class discrimination than the benchmark methods.The findings establish a reproducible benchmark for evaluating CNN-based fraud detection models under severe class imbalance while minimizing the risk of information leakage.

title: Case Studies
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has changed the landscape of marketing in a way that supports the process of data-driven decision-making, personalization, and automation. In this chapter, we will explore case studies showcasing how these AI-driven marketing strategies have changed the way businesses can engage with customers, position their brands, and optimize sales. With predictive analytics, machine learning (ML) algorithms, and natural language processing (NLP), businesses can improve consumer experiences, better target audiences, and generate increased conversions. This examined how AI in marketing is being used in the real world, such as chatbots for customer service, content generation, ad automation, and monitoring of user sentiment. The following examples highlight how AI is actively shaping marketing approaches and enhancing the ROI (return on investment). The articles also mention associated ethical issues like data privacy and biases in algorithms, thus calling for responsible AI deployment. It implies that AI is not just a complementary tool but a core pillar of contemporary marketing, with the power to shift competitive dynamics. Through AI-based insights, organizations will have the ability to create marketing efforts that are more agile, effective, and lead to consistent customer engagement and increased sales. This study adds to the ongoing debate on the impact of AI on marketing innovation and offers practical suggestions for marketers looking to embed AI within their strategic paradigms.

title: Terminal Agents: A Survey of AI Agents in Command-Line Environments
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly act through terminals, yet existing surveys disperse terminal-mediated behavior across software engineering, tool use, and computer-use research. We regard terminal agents as systems whose dominant progress-bearing action--observation loop is mediated by terminal command execution, textual feedback, and stateful environment interaction. Using terminal-mediated execution as an organizing lens, this survey establishes workload-level boundaries and connects system architecture, competence acquisition, and evaluation through a seven-dimensional terminal competence profile. Our synthesis shows that realized behavior is jointly shaped by the model, interface, harness, runtime, and environment. Executable trajectories ground learning in action consequences, verification, and recovery, whereas prevailing evaluations emphasize final outcomes and expose process quality, recovery, and governance unevenly. Bounded fixed-condition diagnostics illustrate two implications: benchmark families expose different process signals, and matched system comparisons reveal benchmark-dependent performance and limits of component attribution. These findings motivate explicit reporting of system and runtime conditions, supported by replayable traces and process-level evidence. The framework provides a unified basis for studying terminal-mediated agency across software engineering and emerging application domains.

title: Garbage Collection and Energy Consumption in Java: A Controlled Study Across Workloads and JDKs
abstract: Garbage-collector selection is a low-effort configuration decision that can influence both the performance and energy consumption of Java applications. However, it remains unclear whether aggregate energy rankings among collectors generalise across heterogeneous applications, workload intensities, and JDK distributions. This study presents a controlled empirical evaluation of Serial, Parallel, and G1 garbage collection across three Java applications, three workload intensities, and two JDK distributions: OpenJDK and Oracle JDK. Using EnergiBridge, processor-package energy consumption and execution time were measured and complementary energy-performance metrics derived. Across all evaluated configurations, Parallel recorded the lowest mean energy consumption (839.8 J), followed closely by Serial (857.6 J) and G1 (969.0 J), but an RCBD ANOVA did not establish a statistically reliable collector effect. Workload intensity, by contrast, was a significant driver of energy consumption, with heavy workloads consuming substantially more energy than light or medium workloads regardless of collector. Energy consumption showed a moderate positive association with execution time (r = 0.33), indicating that longer-running configurations tended toward higher energy use, though the relationship was far from proportional. No statistically significant energy difference was found between OpenJDK and Oracle JDK. Overall, the results do not support a universally energy-optimal garbage collector; instead, workload intensity emerges as the more reliable lever for managing Java energy consumption, and collector selection should be treated as an application-specific tuning decision supported by measurement on the target system rather than aggregate rankings alone.

title: Analisis keluhan publik terhadap Coretax melalui N-Gram pada komentar instagram kementerian keuangan
abstract: This study analyzes public complaints regarding the implementation of the coretax system based on Instagram comments from the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Indonesia posted on October 16, 2025. This study addresses a research gap by applying an N-Gram approach that is exploratory, fast, and efficient in extracting patterns of public complaints specifically from Instagram, which has different interaction characteristics compared to other platforms such as Twitter or online forums. A total of 192 comments were collected through web scraping. Data processing was conducted through text preprocessing stages, including case folding, normalization, stopword removal, tokenization, and stemming. The analysis employed the N-Gram method (unigram, bigram, and trigram) using Python to identify dominant complaint patterns. The results indicate that complaints are primarily related to technical issues such as system errors, access difficulties, and administrative constraints. In addition, the analysis identified increased user workload and dissatisfaction with tax services, particularly near reporting deadlines.

title: Computational Identity Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Identity Theory (CIT), proposing that the true identity of a program resides independently of its underlying code representation. The theory posits that a program, regardless of whether it's implemented in Python, C++, FPGA, or even through quantum execution, constitutes a single computational identity. This challenges traditional understandings of software identity, which typically equate it with the source code. The paper outlines the core principles of CIT, including the concept of Identity-preserving Transformations, and suggests a fundamental re-evaluation of existing compilation theories. The central argument is that the underlying computational process, rather than the specific code, defines the program's essence. The theory is explored through a series of illustrative examples, demonstrating how different implementations can maintain the same computational identity. This work aims to provide a new framework for understanding software identity and its implications across diverse computing paradigms.

title: Computational Identity Algebra
abstract: The field of computer science is rife with notions of "equivalence," yet rarely addresses the fundamental question of what constitutes the "same" computational object. This paper introduces Computational Identity Algebra (CIA), a formal framework designed to rigorously define and analyze identity relationships in computational contexts. CIA provides a mathematical notation, denoted as [ (A, B) ], to represent the identity relation between computational objects A and B. The research presented explores various scenarios, including program modifications, model distillation, and agent replication, to determine whether the objects remain identical after these transformations. The core of CIA rests on establishing a set of axioms and rules governing identity, aiming for a robust and consistent methodology for assessing computational identity. This work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of identity in complex computational systems and opens avenues for applications in areas such as software verification, model management, and autonomous agent coordination. ---
